Building the Right Team to Build Something That Lasts: How Trevor and Kristen Franco Are Growing Vessel Home Services

Vessel Home Services LLC Image Credit: Vessel Home Services LLC

Entrepreneurship often begins with a vision, but building a business that continues creating value over time requires thoughtful leadership and the willingness to grow alongside others. Those principles have shaped Vessel Home Services LLC, where co-founders Trevor and Kristen Franco have built a residential and commercial home services company providing heating, ventilation, air conditioning, refrigeration, installation, maintenance, duct cleaning, and system optimization. 

According to the founders, the company’s growth has centered on acquiring established home service businesses while preserving the relationships, employees, and community trust those companies have built over many years.

Their philosophy aligns with growing recognition that businesses are shaped by the people who lead them. Research shows that managers influence 70% of the variance in employee engagement, highlighting the role leadership plays in building resilient organizations. Trevor says that understanding leadership and culture has become a central part of how Vessel approaches every opportunity, particularly when working alongside family-owned businesses that have spent years earning trust within their communities.

“We’ve always believed that growth comes with responsibility,” Trevor says. “When someone entrusts us with the business they’ve spent years building, our goal is to protect that legacy, support the employees, and continue serving the community that helped make the company successful.”

Kristen says that philosophy also guides how Vessel Home Services evaluates acquisition opportunities. Financial performance matters, but cultural alignment is equally important because the company looks for businesses whose values complement its own long-term approach to customer service and employee development. According to her, the objective is to strengthen existing organizations rather than redefine what made them successful.

As Vessel Home Services expanded through acquisitions, the founders recognized that long-term growth also required expertise beyond their own backgrounds. Trevor brought HVAC experience, while Kristen focused on operations and organizational development. Together, they believed the next stage of growth depended on building a leadership team with complementary perspectives.

“We never expected to have every answer ourselves,” Kristen says. “Building the right team has been just as important as building the business because different experiences help us make better decisions.”

One of those perspectives came through Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer Marquise Boyd, whose Wall Street background introduced a disciplined approach to due diligence and strategic growth. Marquise explains that after years of evaluating businesses from the investment side, he wanted the opportunity to help build one from within, believing Vessel's long-term vision aligned with that goal.

Marquise says his experience analyzing businesses also reinforced the importance of leadership behind financial performance. While his background provided expertise in investment analysis and due diligence, he explains that joining Vessel offered an opportunity to apply those skills within a company whose leadership placed equal importance on people, culture, and long-term relationships.

“My experience taught me that strong businesses begin with strong leadership teams,” Marquise says. “I wanted to help build a company from the inside, and Trevor and Kristen had a vision that focused on creating something sustainable for employees, business owners, and the communities they serve.”

According to Marquise, his outside perspective has strengthened the company’s acquisition process by combining financial discipline with careful evaluation of cultural fit. He notes that every opportunity is assessed not only for operational potential but also for whether the business shares Vessel Homes Services’ values and commitment to customers and employees.

Trevor explains that this philosophy became especially meaningful during the company’s most recent acquisition of another family-owned business. Rather than viewing the transition simply as a change in ownership, Vessel worked to preserve the company’s legacy while supporting its employees and continuing the relationships built with customers over many years.

“Every business has a story,” Trevor says. “Our responsibility is to respect what has already been built while helping create opportunities for the future. When owners know their employees, customers, and legacy will continue to be cared for, that creates confidence throughout the transition.”

That collaborative approach has supported Vessel Home Services’ continued expansion while reinforcing the leadership principles that have guided the company since its founding. Kristen believes the experience offers a broader lesson for entrepreneurs building growing organizations. According to her, sustainable businesses are created by leaders who recognize the value of bringing together people with different expertise but a shared purpose.

“Growth is ultimately about people,” Kristen says. “When you surround yourself with individuals who challenge your thinking, complement your strengths, and believe in the same mission, you create a business that can continue growing long into the future.”

Could Increasing Immune-IQ™ Help Reduce the Risk of Chronic Disease and Support Healthy Aging?

Image Credit: Alex Blyth

Alex Blyth, inventor, biologist, economist, and biotech entrepreneur, points to a query he believes deserves greater attention: Why does the immune system allow the bodily systems and cell quality to decline with age and ultimately develop chronic and fatal diseases? Through his work in oncology, immunology, and longevity science, he has observed patterns suggesting that important signals often emerge long before conventional diagnosis. “Why do we wait until people are sick before we act?” Blyth asks. “A more valuable question may be how early we can understand that the body is beginning to decline, and what the best lead indicators are for that.”

That perspective has been shaped by more than two decades in life sciences. Having worked across biotechnology innovation, healthcare strategy, and immunotherapy development, Blyth became increasingly interested in the mechanisms that influence long-term health before disease becomes visible. “My work in cancer and other emerging research is increasingly suggesting that bodily decline follows immune decline. The immune system may play roles beyond defending against infections, potentially helping the body maintain stability and address various internal changes. I believe that when aspects of this system become less effective, this could contribute to the accumulation of biological ‘errors,’ which might be associated with conditions often seen with aging, such as certain cancers, cardiovascular issues, cognitive decline, or autoimmune tendencies,” Blyth says. 

He notes that current clinical tools, such as a full White Blood Cell Count, mainly provide information about the numbers of different immune cells rather than offering a broad picture of how well those cells might be functioning. What he believes is needed is an all‑encompassing way to assess the immune competence of different white blood cells against different threats (cancers, aged cells, viruses) and friends (healthy cells, foods, friendly bacteria). 

Through Viternity and its Immune-IQ™ platform, he is exploring how advances in artificial intelligence and immune analytics could enable individuals to better predict disease and understand at a cellular level what in the immune system needs to be fixed to prevent it. “If you can fix the immune system, it can then get back to fixing you,” Blyth points out. 

The timing of this conversation is significant. The World Health Organization reports that noncommunicable diseases accounted for 75% of all non-pandemic-related deaths, with cardiovascular disease, cancer, metabolic disorders, and related chronic conditions representing the largest share. Meanwhile, a McKinsey industry report suggests that although people are living longer, many now spend more years managing illness, prompting growing interest in strategies that support healthy years of life alongside longevity. 

For Blyth, this reflects a broader characteristic of modern medicine. “I’ve seen healthcare systems achieve remarkable advances in diagnosis and treatment, but much of their infrastructure still focuses on identifying and managing disease after symptoms emerge,” he says. “While this reactive model has delivered substantial benefits thus far, particularly for acute conditions, the next era of preventing chronic disease requires a more pre-emptive approach because of the longer biological timelines involved.” 

That distinction matters to Blyth because biological and immune dysfunction may begin years before visible illness. Earlier visibility, he emphasizes, could create opportunities for more informed decision-making, improved quality of life, and potentially lower long-term healthcare burdens. According to the same report, preventive interventions account for a substantial share of the health gains that could be achieved globally by 2050, highlighting the growing importance of earlier action.

“Recent advances in AI, computational biology, and large-scale health data have expanded what may be possible,” Blyth says. Instead of focusing exclusively on disease detection, he notes that researchers can increasingly examine patterns associated with biological risk, resilience, and decline. He regards this transition as an important development. “The future of healthcare may involve understanding where a person is heading biologically, not simply documenting where they are today,” he adds.

Within that framework, the immune system occupies a central role in his thinking. Blyth views immune competence as one of the body’s earliest monitoring functions that can potentially evaluate tissues, identify abnormalities, coordinate repair, and remove cellular debris. He argues that shifts in immune performance may offer valuable insight into future health trajectories. 

Blyth illustrates this concept through the idea of the immune system as a maintenance network. According to him, when that network functions efficiently, damaged or aging cells are identified and cleared. As immune performance changes over time, those processes may become less effective, allowing biological dysfunction to accumulate. “The immune system is constantly making decisions,” Blyth explains. “Health may depend heavily on how accurately it distinguishes friend from foe and how proportionately it responds.”

This philosophy forms the foundation of Immune-IQ™, an AI-enabled platform designed to evaluate immune competence and integrate it with broader biological data. Drawing from functional assays, immune biomarkers, genetics, epigenetic signals, microbiome information, imaging, and other health inputs, the platform seeks to create a more comprehensive picture of an individual's biological status. Blyth believes that this type of analysis may help identify patterns associated with future disease risk five to 10 years before conventional diagnostics would typically detect them.

An important aspect of the platform involves understanding immune balance. Excessive immune activity may contribute to chronic inflammation and autoimmune conditions, while insufficient surveillance may reduce the body’s ability to recognize infections, abnormal cells, and other threats. Blyth argues that both sides of this equation matter. “Health is not simply about activating the immune system or suppressing it,” he says. “It is about helping the system make better decisions, and that is why we call it Immune-IQ™.”

This emphasis on personalization also reflects his concerns about broad, one-size-fits-all longevity strategies. As public interest in dietary supplements and peptides grows, Blyth believes the biological context becomes increasingly important. AI, he notes, offers a way to analyze complex combinations of variables and support more individualized recommendations based on a person’s unique biological profile, rather than taking supplement stacks that may work against what the actual problem is.

Blyth uses the current interest in anti‑inflammatory supplements and medications as an example, suggesting that while reducing inflammation can be helpful in certain situations, it may not always be straightforward. “If inflammation isn’t resolving after an initial trigger, some people might see a rationale for trying to lower it,” he says. “But if the inflammation were linked to something like an undetected condition or a less active immune response, then dampening that response could be viewed differently.” 

As predictive healthcare continues to evolve, Blyth sees the convergence of immune science, AI, and preventive medicine creating new possibilities for extending healthspan. After all, expanding access to proven preventive interventions could generate substantial health and economic benefits over the coming decades.

Overall, Blyth emphasizes that the next major advance in medicine may emerge from understanding biological dysfunction while meaningful opportunities for intervention still exist. In his view, Immune-IQ™ could become one of the most valuable indicators of future health, and a cornerstone of the next era of disease prevention and immune-rejuvenation medicines.

The Compliance Gap Nobody is Talking About, And How to Close It

Dinesh Singh, founder of Acumen Bay Image source: Acumen Bay

Somewhere between the boardroom and the shop floor, most organizations tend to lose control of compliance. Dinesh Singh, founder of Acumen Bay, argues that this dynamic rarely emerges after a single dramatic failure, but is rather a culmination of a thousand small gaps, from an inspection recorded on paper and never actioned, never even questioned. Individually, these may appear trivial. Collectively, Singh defines them as the difference between an organization that knows what is happening inside and one that is merely hoping. 

“We are entering a decade in which hope is no longer a strategy. Regulators appear to be raising the bar on which businesses must prove, not claim, but prove, about how safely and responsibly they operate, and the obligations are rising faster than most organizations’ ability to meet them,” Singh explains. That gap, between what is required and what companies can demonstrate, is the defining operational risk of today, according to him.

He points to the first binding climate law drawn by the United Arab Emirates, requiring some entities that generate emissions to measure, report, and reduce them. “There is no size threshold and no sector exemption; the first deadline falls in 2026, and failure carries fines running into the millions,” Singh notes. “For businesses that have never measured a tonne of carbon, this is a standing start.”

The UAE, he adds, isn’t an outlier but a signal. 

Qatar, Chile, and Mexico are a few countries planning to adopt disclosure rules in the future, and Singh explains that the emerging global baseline standards for climate reporting have now been aligned in more than two dozen jurisdictions representing over half the world’s economy. Even in Europe, where recent reforms narrowed formal requirements to the largest companies, Singh believes the pressure ripples down the supply chain, impacting smaller firms that are still asked for the data.  

He notes that the pattern is what matters. Whether the demand comes from a regulator, a bank, an insurer, or a customer’s contract, Singh believes the direction is identical, with continuous, evidenced, and auditable proof of how companies operate. “Leadership understands the importance of compliance, sustainability, and health and safety, but the real challenge is making sure those priorities become consistent actions across the organization,” he says. 

Compliance, as Singh puts it, is a set of things that either happen or don’t, every day inside an operation. Did the inspection get done, and did anyone act on what it found? When a machine failed, was it logged and fixed, or quietly worked around? When a customer complained, did it trigger a real investigation? According to Singh, these are the raw materials of every audit and regulatory inspection, and in most organizations, they often live in a chaos of spreadsheets, email threads, paper forms, and individual memory.

Singh argues that this shift carries particular significance for small and medium-sized businesses. Large enterprises often have dedicated compliance functions and specialist teams to navigate evolving requirements. Growing businesses, he argues, may not always have that advantage. However, Singh adds that regulators often balance this by introducing size thresholds and proportionate obligations. 

At the same time, he argues that large organizations can still harbour vulnerability. According to him, sophisticated headquarters can mask near-total operational blindness at lower-tier depots. While organizational scale provides resources, Singh notes that it may also breed fragmentation. In his view, the common thread, at every scale, is a shortage of visibility. 

Although that reality can appear daunting, Singh believes it should encourage organizations to strengthen the way they function instead of viewing compliance as another burden placed on the business. “Compliance should be treated as an advantage. When it becomes part of everyday operations, it can strengthen accountability and decision-making and support long-term business growth,” Singh explains. 

Those same principles shaped the development of Audit-Here, Acumen Bay’s cloud-based, end-to-end compliance SaaS platform. Instead of expecting frontline employees to become compliance specialists, the platform was designed to support the individuals already responsible for inspections, maintenance faults, audits, and operational activities by helping digitize and manage internal audits, safety incidents, risk and hazard assessments, and both global & local regulatory frameworks in a single system. “Management should be able to see and govern what’s happening through evidence, not speculation,” he adds. 

Similarly, Singh notes that everything true of safety and quality now applies to sustainability, where he believes that the knowledge gap is even wider. The willingness to comply often exists, but the knowledge required to organize and report meaningful data is often limited.

Acumen Bay developed Green-Here, another intuitive SaaS platform to address that challenge by helping businesses transform existing operational information into structured sustainability reporting. The platform is designed with the aim of establishing emissions baselines, tracking their ESG targets, and building practical reduction plans aligned with evolving regulatory frameworks.

In Singh’s view, sustainability reporting delivers its greatest value after the report has been completed. He believes organizations should understand their carbon footprint with the same confidence they understand their financial performance. In that process, Singh believes that leaders could identify opportunities to reduce energy costs and strengthen long-term profitability.

“Green-Here puts the data back in the organization’s own hands, guiding it through simple user interface, capturing emissions across every source that makes up its footprint, fuel, energy, refrigerants, water, travel, freight, materials, and the value chain, and replacing the annual guess with a continuous, auditable inventory of the kind regulators now demand,” he says. 

As compliance expectations continue to evolve, Singh believes organizations will distinguish themselves by how effectively they integrate compliance into everyday operations. Businesses that improve operational visibility today, he asserts, will be better positioned to strengthen governance and support sustainable growth over the long term.

Building Solutions That Last

Japanese manufacturers are responding to demand for high value-added components. For Osaka’s Takenaka Seisakusho, years of R&D and collaborations with institutions such as Kyoto University have led to the development of TAKECOAT®-1000, the world’s first fluoropolymer specifically for bolts. In environments where seawater corrosion is common, such as oil platforms and pipelines, this innovation is a game-changer. Its importance in these regions can’t be overstated. “We have been focusing on overseas markets for over 30 years, responding to global business trends. TAKECOAT® meets the national oil specifications in the UAE and Saudi Arabia, and we are working hard to meet customer needs, including expansion into local markets,” President Saeko Takenaka explained.

Takenaka is also mindful of how her company can contribute to society. “We have an ongoing project to introduce more environmentally friendly products. I truly hope, as a member of modern society, that we can contribute more and more to a greener, healthier future, and we aim to do this by improving not only our products but also our production methods. Environmentally friendly monozukuri will remain a big priority for us as much as continuing to innovate,” she said.
